title: Dhammadinna answers
hookLine: a nun answers her former husband's questions; the Buddha says he would have answered the same
tomorrow: Four ways of taking things on

lines: THE COMMENTARIES: HE WAS HER HUSBAND.
NOW SHE'S THE ONE WHO KNOWS.
cards: A layman named Visakha walks up to a nun named Dhammadinna, bows, and sits to one side. He has questions, hard ones. The discourse doesn't say anything else about the two of them.

But the later commentaries tell a story behind it: Visakha had been Dhammadinna's husband. When he turned to the path, she asked to go forth as a nun, and he let her. Now he's the one asking, and she's the one who knows.

teach.b: In the shorter discourse of questions and answers, the forty-fourth of the Middle-Length Sayings, Visakha asks and Dhammadinna answers, one after another, without hesitating. What is identity, the sense of a self?
Clinging to the five aggregates, she says: body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. How does that sense of self arise? From craving.
How does it end? When craving ends. Then about meditation.
What are the formations of the body? The in-breath and out-breath. Of speech?
Thinking things over, because we think before we speak. Of the mind? Perception and feeling.
Then about feeling. Pleasant feeling, she says, has a hidden tendency toward desire. Painful feeling, toward aversion.
Neutral feeling, toward ignorance. Visakha keeps going, deeper and deeper, until he asks what nibbana's counterpart is. And she stops him kindly.
You've gone too far, friend Visakha. You couldn't find the end of your questions. The holy life merges in nibbana and ends in it.
If you like, go and ask the Buddha. He does, and reports the whole conversation. And the Buddha says: Dhammadinna is wise.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA: SHE ANSWERED AS I WOULD
teach.b: If you had asked me, I would have answered exactly as she did.
That is the meaning, and you should remember it that way. A teacher saying a woman disciple's answers are his answers. Her words sit in the canon as teaching, with the Buddha's own seal on them.

how: Theravada tradition remembers Dhammadinna as the nun foremost among those who teach the Dhamma, and MN 44 is studied as a compact teaching on self, feeling and meditation; it is cited today in discussions of women as teachers.

o: a list of rules written for Buddhist nuns
a nun's answers that the Buddha made his own
a husband's gift to a newly ordained wife

s: the sutta itself says Visakha was her former husband
the sutta doesn't say; the later commentaries tell that story.
the Buddha said he would have answered the same way
he called her wise and told Visakha to remember the meaning as she gave it.
Dhammadinna answered every question, however far it went
when he asked for nibbana's counterpart, she told him he'd gone too far.

games.q: you're Dhammadinna. your questioner keeps going deeper and asks: what is the counterpart of nibbana? what do you do?
o: tell him he's gone too far, and send him to the Buddha if he likes.
refuse to speak to him again.
games.why: she stops him kindly: he couldn't find the limit of his questions. the holy life ends in nibbana. then he takes it all to the Buddha, who agrees with her.

practice: Think of someone who taught you something real without looking like a teacher, a younger sibling, a coworker, a child, someone you once underestimated, and let gratitude come.
Then try Dhammadinna's answer about feeling: notice one feeling in the body, and whether there's a lean toward it, a lean away, or a fog.

wordCard.voice: Dhammadinna answers. A nun's teaching on self, breath and feeling, which the Buddha called his own.

orig.note: Pali vedana: feeling, pleasant, painful or neither. Dhammadinna explains the tendency hidden in each.

carryVoice: Your line: I'd have said the same. A good answer is good, whoever gives it. Until tomorrow.
